newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Visitors to see double in German culture capital.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Visitors to see double in German culture capital.

text.p: Visitors to one of Germany's most historic cities may be seeing double in a couple of years -- and it has nothing to do with the local beer.
Right next to Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's old summer house in Weimar, officials plan to build an exact replica.
The idea is just one of many which Weimar has up its sleeve for 1999, when it will be Europe's City of Culture.

Not only did Germany's most famous poet, novelist and playwright spend most of his life in Weimar, it was also the home of Schiller, Bach, Liszt and Nietzsche. The renowned Bauhaus movement of design and architecture began in Weimar.

Bernd Kauffmann, a flamboyant west German in charge of the 1999 programme, is determined not to organise a strait-laced festival which simply reveres Weimar's past, as the summer house project demonstrates.
For Kauffmann, the attraction is to see how people react in the replica, faced with exact copies of Goethe's piano, armchair and even his bed.
"They can touch everything they're not allowed to in the original," he enthused. "They can feel for themselves."
For good measure, he also plans a triplicate version -- in cyberspace. Internet surfers will be able to stroll through the house by the Ilm river without leaving their armchairs.
"People have said I'm doing this for tourism but I'm not," Kauffmann said. "Attracting tourists is, maybe, a small secondary argument for doing this, but not the main one."
But there is more to this city than the house where Goethe spent most of his life, the summer residence across the river and the Nationaltheater where many of his works were first performed.
SINISTER PAST
Weimar was also the home of Buchenwald concentration camp.
Rather than trying to keep the dark side of the city's history out of sight when Weimar spends a year in the spotlight, Kauffmann plans to put it at the centre of his 1999 programme.

For him, Weimar is a unique symbol of both the highs and lows of the German psyche -- from the genius of Goethe to the barbarism of the Nazis. He plans to underscore the paradox with several prominent projects.

Kauffmann wants to clear an overgrown forest path between Buchenwald, now a museum to the Nazi horrors it witnessed, and Schloss Ettersburg, the baroque summer residence of Duchess Anna Amalia, a keen patron of the arts in Goethe's day.

Weimar will also host an exhibition of works by artists imprisoned at Buchenwald while contemporary artists will highlight the physical links -- such as railway lines, roads and cemeteries -- between the city and the camp on its outskirts.

Grand plans come cheap. Turning them into reality is an expensive business. The European Union bestows the title City of Culture but little money. Weimar itself, like most former East German cities coming to terms with capitalism, has no cash.
This means Kauffmann has to rely largely on money from the federal and regional governments and sponsorship from private companies. None has been as generous as he would like.
"I've yet to receive a promise of anything from a single major company," he complains, although insisting the culture programme is not in financial crisis.

The whole project is made more difficult and costly by the legacy of communist East German rule -- a lack of established independent cultural institutions and crumbling buildings badly in need of renovation.
The regional government has pledged 76.5 million marks ($49.21 million) to restore the city's historic buildings to their former glory.
"People in the West curse Weimar for being how it is," Kauffmann says. "But they forget they've had 40 years of cultural foundations, of restorations and renovations. Weimar has to catch up."
The citizens of Weimar seem happy enough that their city is to be honoured in a couple of years but less keen on Kauffmann's plan to duplicate their beloved house on the banks of the Ilm.
"It should stay as it is. It doesn't deserve all these silly games," said Manfred Schueler, an engineer walking with his wife in the park next to Goethe's old haunt.

"It's not beautiful but it's unique," said secretary Elisabeth Lattke, adding that visitors were allowed to touch objects in the original in the old East German days. "It's an idyllic place and they should leave it in peace."
Others may not be bursting with enthusiasm but are willing to keep an open mind about the duplicate, on the grounds it can always be torn down if it proves unpopular.
"We should be open to new experiments and we have to do something to control the number of visitors to the house in 1999," said Britta Lorenz, a teacher walking her dog.
"I was sceptical about the idea but I'm in favour of an experiment. We'll see how people react."
Kauffmann is hoping visitors from outside the city will be more receptive to his plan. But he insists his aim is not to attract as many people as possible.
The amount of time they spend in Weimar is more important than the overall number, he says.
"I hope people come for longer. We don't need day trippers who tear through the city drinking beer and eating sausages." ($1=1.5544 Mark)
